title: The 2028 extension: rates and fund credits for one more year, with a transfer keeping both accounts solvent through FY2031 (a 2027-28 exception)
parameters: A labeled 2027-28 exception: it is enacted before the plan's January 2029 start, by Sept 30, 2028, and needs a bipartisan 60-vote regular bill under divided government. (1) Extend 26 U.S.C. 9503(b) and (e) and the expiring rates one year, to Sept 30, 2029, with no change to the Mass Transit Account's 2.86 cents and no merger of the accounts (the Secretary's July 2026 proposal to eliminate the Mass Transit Account is not adopted). (2) A general-fund transfer that keeps both accounts solvent through FY2031; the transfer is not yet sized. Reconciliation cannot make an intragovernmental transfer later (Byrd rule), and BUILD America 250-Plus's proposed $108.0B transfer covers only CBO's shortfall through FY2030 (CBO's end-FY2031 shortfalls under H.R. 8870 are $99.5B highway and $48.2B transit, assuming the expiring taxes continue; a cash-flow model is needed to size it). (3) Extend the heavy-vehicle use tax to Sept 30, 2030, so it runs until the weight-distance charge starts (Draft 2's vehicle table at L24 omits this; L208 and L1830 include it; this provision follows the longer text). No new revenue in FY2029: FY2029 receipts are current-law rates, $49.3B. New rates start Oct 1, 2029 (fuel), Oct 1, 2030 (per-mile charges, trucks, rail diesel at 10 and 5 cents) and Oct 1, 2031 (aviation; rail diesel at 15 and 7.5 cents). Why a one-year extension: it keeps 2029's forcing event, an expiring tax base to reform. A-9 (3-design.md, point 2, decided as recommended). Not modelled: the case with no extension, or one that runs past FY2029 (the forcing event is lost, though reconciliation can still raise rates).
eligibility: Owners and users of the taxed fuels, vehicles and trips; no income test (transportation has no income-tested benefit); the transfer pays the Highway and Mass Transit Accounts

title: Fuel taxes permanent and indexed, with ten 3-cent Fix-It-First steps and a gas-price pause (MR1; 2029 act)
parameters: Act: the 2029 reconciliation act (vehicle R1); effective for removals, entries and sales after Sept 30, 2029 (MR1; A-10; memo 1 option A; Draft 2 div. A sec. 103(a)-(d), (f)). (1) Strike 26 U.S.C. 4081(d)(1), so the rates are permanent. (2) New 4081(a)(2)(E): for fiscal years beginning after Sept 30, 2029 the rate is the clause rate plus the Fix-It-First amount plus the fossil transition amount (MOV-29.02), multiplied by 1 plus the cost-of-living adjustment, rounded to the nearest 0.1 cent, never lower than the prior year. The adjustment is CPI-U for the 12 months ending June 30 against the 12 months ending June 30, 2028 (indexed from FY2030). (3) Fix-It-First amount: 3 cents times the number of steps taken, at most 10; one step on Oct 1, 2029 and one each Oct 1 after, until 10. (4) Price pause: no step in a year if the EIA average retail regular gasoline price for the 12 months ending June 30 exceeded $4.00 times 1 plus that October's adjustment, or exceeded the preceding 12-month average by more than 20 percent; a deferred step is taken on the first Oct 1 that neither test applies, never more than one step on an Oct 1 (deferred, not forfeited). Other fuels under 26 U.S.C. 4041 follow. (5) Permanent fund credits and expenditure authority: strike 'before October 1, 2028' in 9503(b)(1), conform (b)(2), strike the expenditure end dates in 9503(c)(1) and (e)(3) and refer to divisions A-D. Draft 2 notes the dates assume the 2028 extension carries credits only to Sept 30, 2029 (MOV-28.01). Cost to drivers: a 25-mpg car driven 12,000 miles pays $88 a year now, $105 in FY2030, $142 in FY2032 and $225 in FY2036; with no pause gasoline reaches 62.0 cents nominal in FY2039, 48.4 cents in 2029 dollars, against 45.3 cents for the 1993 rate in 2029 dollars (other Draft 2 passages say 'about 48 cents' and 'near where 1993 left it'; the 48.4 / 45.3 pair governs). Receipts FY2032-36: $426.7B of fuel tax (gasoline $294.2B, diesel $132.5B). Alternatives weighed (memo 1): indexing only (draw 0.267% of GDP; coverage in FY2042-46 62 / 42 / 75), 2-cent steps (0.209%; 85 / 88 / 111), three pauses (0.204%, recovered later; about $53.3B of FY2032-36 receipts). Model has no demand response (probably 2-3% of fuel receipts). Score: +$380.4B gross over FY2029-38 for indexing and steps.
eligibility: Owners and users of the taxed fuels, vehicles and trips; no income test (transportation has no income-tested benefit)

title: The fossil transition premium, FY2040-44 (A-28; MR1; enacted in 2029, scores nothing inside either window)
parameters: Act: the 2029 reconciliation act (R1); memo 1 option A; Draft 2 div. A sec. 103(b) (new 4081(a)(2)(E)(iv), (v)) and sec. 101(l), (m). Fossil transition amount: 2 cents times the number of transition steps, at most 5, one step each Oct 1 not earlier than Oct 1, 2039 and only after all ten Fix-It-First steps are taken; the same price pause applies. Clean vehicles pay the road-use rate (the rate without the fossil transition amount, 4081(a)(2)(E)(v)), never the premium. Receipts are credited outside the sec. 101(c)-(d) split, in proportion to each account's projected excess of obligations over other receipts in the latest report under div. A sec. 108(a) (MOV-31.08), and by the 35/50/15 or 45/40/15 shares if there is no report (the report exists only if the 2031 bill is law). Policy statement (sec. 101(m)): reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Effect: it starts in FY2040, outside both reconciliation windows, so the acts score nothing for it. Receipts: $16.3B in FY2037-41 and $124.8B in FY2042-46, an upper bound because the model has no demand response and a premium meant to move drivers off fossil fuel shrinks its own base. Without it FY2042-46 draws 0.065% of GDP instead of 0.026%, and renewal coverage (highway / transit / rail) is 89 / 96 / 104 instead of 95 / 109 / 135 (Draft 2's A-8 line quotes 89 / 96 / 104 without saying it excludes the premium; the base case with the premium is 95 / 109 / 135). Crediting by need is insurance: credited by the regular split it stranded $28.9B in transit under a 25-mpg peg. Alternatives: no premium; a larger, open-ended one.
eligibility: Owners and users of the taxed fuels, vehicles and trips; no income test (transportation has no income-tested benefit) (gasoline and diesel users; clean vehicles exempt)

title: The clean-vehicle per-mile charge, odometer base only (MR2; A-11; 2029 act, starts Oct 1, 2030)
parameters: Act: the 2029 reconciliation act (R1); memo 1 option A; Draft 2 div. A sec. 102 (new 26 U.S.C. 4491-4493, subchapter E of chapter 36). Rate per mile: for a covered vehicle of 26,000 lb gross vehicle weight or less, the gasoline road-use rate on Oct 1 of the fiscal year divided by 40; for a plug-in hybrid, 30 percent of that; for any other covered vehicle, the diesel road-use rate divided by 6.5. Parity is with what an efficient (40-mpg) gas car pays to keep roads funded, never with the fossil premium, so no clean car pays more per mile than a 40-mpg hybrid. Covered: battery-electric (external recharge) or fuel-cell vehicles. Exempt: the United States, States and political subdivisions, tribal governments, public transportation. No tax on miles before Oct 1, 2030 (a year after enactment, to give Treasury and the States time to build collection). Base (4492): the difference between odometer readings at registration, renewal, inspection or an owner-submitted reading, for a period of not more than 15 months; no location data (the bar and the retention rules are in the 2031 bill, MOV-31.11, because reconciliation may not carry them; readings are return information under 26 U.S.C. 6103 from the first day, so the gap is narrow, and Draft 2 suggests a standalone privacy bill before Oct 1, 2030 to close it; that is Draft 2's suggestion, not a plan commitment). Payment (4493): annual; State agreements remit not less than 99 percent of collections within 60 days; a cost allowance of not more than 10 percent of collections, not credited to the Fund. Credited to the fund under 9503(b)(1)(F). Implementation: $750,000,000 to Treasury, available until Sept 30, 2033, for systems and State agreements; $25,000,000 to DOT for a highway cost allocation study by class, weight and axle configuration, due to Ways and Means and Finance by March 31, 2030. Amounts: 0.64 cents a mile in FY2031 ($77 a year at 12,000 miles), 1.17 cents in FY2036 ($141, equal to a 40-mpg hybrid) and 1.84 cents in FY2046 ($221, against $267 for the hybrid and $427 for a 25-mpg car); a plug-in driven 40% on electricity pays about $126 in FY2036. Receipts FY2032-36: $14.5B (cars $8.5B, trucks $6.0B). Alternative weighed: pegging to 25 mpg with plug-ins at 50% (about $5.7B more in FY2032-36). Score: +$16.5B (cars) and +$12.9B (trucks) over FY2029-38.
eligibility: Owners of battery-electric, fuel-cell and plug-in hybrid vehicles; no income test

title: The three-account fund and its shares of new revenue: 35 / 50 / 15 (2029 act); 45 / 40 / 15 from FY2037 is in the 2031 bill (MOV-31.01)
parameters: Act: the 2029 reconciliation act (R1), revenue title; Draft 2 div. A sec. 101 (a)-(f), (h), (j)-(m); memo 3 option A (A-7). (a) Redesignate the Highway Trust Fund in 26 U.S.C. 9503 as the Surface Transportation Trust Fund. (b) Accounts: Highway Account, Mass Transit Account (9503(e)), Intercity Passenger Rail Account. (c) Base amounts: for FY2029 and after, the amount credited for FY2028 increased by the percentage change in CPI-U since FY2028 is credited first to the Highway and Mass Transit Accounts; pro rata if receipts fall short. (d)(1) New revenue above the base, FY2029-2036: 35 percent Highway, 50 percent Mass Transit, 15 percent Intercity Passenger Rail. The FY2037 shares (d)(2), 45 / 40 / 15 'unless a later Act provides otherwise after the report under subsection (i)', are added by the 2031 bill (MOV-31.01), not by this act. (e) Rail-specific receipts (the 4283 aviation surcharge and the 4041(a)(1)(C)(ii) rail diesel rates (IV) and (V)) are credited to the Rail Account outside (c) and (d). (f) Renewal first: account amounts are available for expansion programs only to the extent they exceed renewal amounts; expansion = CIG (5309), div. C sec. 606, div. D secs. 303, 310, 311, 312 and the readiness reserve; renewal = every Highway Account program, Mass Transit Account chapter 53 programs and the rest of div. C, and Rail Account programs other than expansion; div. B sec. 1112 is neither (A-19, one renewal definition for all three accounts). (h) Rail Account subaccounts in div. D sec. 101(b). (j) Policy: federal assistance for intercity rail and public transportation combined equals highways by FY2045 ('federal assistance' is not defined; FY2032-36 already shows transit plus rail $475.45B against highways $461.12B). (k) committees; (l) fossil transition receipts as in MOV-29.02. Why 35 / 50 / 15: the incremental shares (A-7, decided); the equal-coverage solve (50.0 / 38.2 / 11.8) is the alternative, and the move to 45 / 40 / 15 in FY2037 is A-8. Kept forever, the first split leaves transit $5.9B it cannot spend while highway renewal coverage sits at 80% in FY2042-46; with the move nothing is stranded. The split does not change the general-fund draw; it decides which account reaches self-sufficiency first. Not in this act: striking 'capital' from 9503(e)(3) (sec. 101(g)), which has no budgetary effect and rides in the 2031 bill (the Draft 2 section index lists all of sec. 101 as '2029 act'; its Byrd table puts 101(g) in the 2031 bill; this provision follows the Byrd table). Dedicated receipts by account FY2032-36: highways $321.19B, transit $154.27B, rail $70.38B.
eligibility: Accounts of the fund; no individuals

title: Renewal top-ups for FY2032-34, plus FY2035 highway and transit: $209.74B, with their deadlines (A-14, A-15; 2029 act)
parameters: Act: the 2029 reconciliation act (R1); point 3 of 3-design.md (A-14, A-15); Draft 2 'Renewal top-ups' table (L280-294). The renewal shortfall that dedicated receipts cannot yet cover reaches programs directly, not through the fund: reconciliation cannot make a general-fund transfer into a trust fund (Byrd rule), so top-ups are general-fund appropriations to existing programs. Highway (title 23 formula programs): $28.55B FY2032, $28.47B FY2033, $28.20B FY2034, $27.72B FY2035 = $112.94B, limited to preservation, rehabilitation, reconstruction or replacement (fix-it-first in practice). Transit (49 U.S.C. 5307, 5337, 5339, 5311): $14.04B, $11.01B, $7.68B, $3.96B = $36.69B (transit's top-up reaches zero in FY2036). Rail (Amtrak grants, 24911, 22907, 22909): $20.60B FY2032, $20.44B FY2033, $19.07B FY2034 = $60.11B. FY2035 highway and transit together are $31.68B. Total $209.74B. Placing top-ups by fiscal year (FY2032-34 / FY2035-36) would add about $27.5B to deficits in the 2030 act and fail the Byrd out-year test without offsets. Locking top-ups in 2029-30 means the 60-vote 2031 bill carries only expansion appropriations, and renewal funding survives if the 2031 bill stalls or the 2030 midterms end the trifecta. The distribution among programs inside each mode is made by div. A sec. 110(b) (MOV-31.10) in the 2031 bill, so until then this act's text names the programs. title: A weight-distance charge for trucks over 26,000 lb, replacing the heavy-vehicle use tax (MR4; A-12; 2030 act, starts Oct 1, 2030)
parameters: Act: the 2030 reconciliation act (vehicle R3); memo 2 option A; Draft 2 div. A sec. 104(a), (b) (new 26 U.S.C. 4495; 4481). Charge on a highway motor vehicle with a declared combined gross weight over 26,000 pounds, per mile on U.S. public highways. FY2031 rate per mile: 0.8 cent for a declared weight of not more than 33,000 lb; 1.6 cents for more than 33,000 up to 55,000; 2.6 cents for more than 55,000 up to 70,000; 3.4 cents for more than 70,000 up to 80,000; and 3.4 cents plus 0.4 cent for each 2,000 lb or fraction over 80,000. Vehicles with fewer than 5 axles over 55,000 lb pay 125 percent. Indexed by the cost-of-living adjustment relative to FY2031. Miles come from IFTA distance records or odometer readings, on quarterly returns under State IFTA agreements: the filings carriers already make. Intrastate carriers, which file no IFTA return, report odometer miles once a year on the annual return that replaces the 4481 use tax, with the declared weight their State registration records (a working choice for the 2030 act's drafting; a new line for trucks of 55,000 lb or more, which already file the annual use-tax return, and a new filing for those between 26,000 and 55,000 lb). It applies in addition to the clean-vehicle charge for zero-emission trucks (4491(b)(3)), so clean trucks pay both. No tax on miles before Oct 1, 2030. The heavy-vehicle use tax: 4481(f) 'October 1, 2029' becomes 'October 1, 2030' and 4481 does not apply to use after Sept 30, 2030 (the 2028 extension carries it to that date, MOV-28.01). Credited under 9503(b)(1)(G). Calibration: about a 3-cent average across Class 7-8 miles (about $6.4B in FY2031); the final schedule is set by the 2030 act from the cost allocation study ordered in MOV-29.03 (due March 31, 2030). Example: an 80,000-lb tractor running 100,000 miles pays about $3,400 a year in place of the $550 use tax, plus the diesel steps. Receipts FY2032-36: $35.8B. Alternatives weighed: a 2-cent average (draw 0.185% of GDP average, all-in peak 0.213%); a diesel increase alone; keeping the use tax. Experience: Oregon's weight-mile tax costs about 11% of revenue to collect against 0.3% for fuel tax, and a 2021 study put evasion at roughly 5-11% of revenue [EV-MOV-118] [EV-MOV-122], which is why the evaluation in div. E sec. 103 (MOV-31.82) reports collection cost and evasion yearly. Score: +$67.3B weight-distance and -$13.9B use tax repealed (FY2030-39).
eligibility: Owners and operators of trucks over 26,000 lb; no income test

title: The contingency authorization: if no multi-year surface transportation law is in place by Dec 31, 2028, a regular-order authorization in 2029-30, with highway title I drafted in full
parameters: Vehicle: a regular bill, 60 votes, in 2029-30; decided as recommended (point 1 of 3-design.md). Trigger: no multi-year surface transportation authorization is law on Dec 31, 2028 (baseline case 2, short extensions through 2028, or case 3, a lapse on Oct 1, 2028; the scenario dossier puts a multi-year bill by the end of 2028 at 40-55%, so this authorization is about as likely as not to be needed). Content: an authorization covering the years to FY2031, written by regular order alongside or after the 2029 act, with division B's highway title I drafted in full (MOV-31.20 and MOV-31.21 otherwise adopt H.R. 8870's title I by reference, which assumes it was enacted), and with the transit and rail programs it needs for those years at roughly current levels (case 2) or to restart them (case 3). The 2031 bill (MOV-31.01 to MOV-31.89, effective Oct 1, 2031) then becomes its renewal for FY2032-36. Why: the reconciliation acts cannot authorize programs (Byrd rule), so without this the top-up and package money (MOV-29.06 to MOV-29.09, MOV-30.04 to MOV-30.06) has no programs to flow to in FY2029-31. The design text names the years as FY2029-31 or FY2030-34; this provision follows the brief's years-to-FY2031 and leaves levels to section 6, which states which case it prices. The 2029 and 2030 acts work in every case, because they set revenue and top up existing programs; only the 2031 bill's timing changes. Not priced here; the cost depends on the case.
